fixture.body: Say the hour first, then the minutes: 7:05 is seven oh five, and o'clock follows only a full hour: seven o'clock. Point Rule Example Asking answer with It's + the time What time is it? — It's seven thirty. Numbers say the hour, then the minutes; 1–9 minutes take oh 7:05 → seven oh five o'clock a full hour takes o'clock seven o'clock past minutes 1–30: past the hour five past three / (a) quarter past three / half past three to minutes 31–59: to the next hour; say the minutes first twenty to four / (a) quarter to four minutes minutes that are not 5, 10, 15… add minutes three minutes past six a.m. / p.m. a.m. is midnight to midday; p.m. is midday to midnight seven a.m. / three p.m. Parts of the day add the part of the day after the time seven in the morning / three in the afternoon / eight in the evening / eleven at night 24 hours speech uses 12 hours; timetables use the 24-hour clock 19:30 → nineteen thirty US use after for past and of for to a quarter after three / ten of four Approximate times about, nearly and just gone before the time; on the dot after it about half past three / seven o'clock on the dot Trap minutes replace o'clock seven fifteen The time in numbers Ask What time is it? or What's the time? Answer with It's + the time. It's seven thirty. Time Said 7:00 seven o'clock 7:05 seven oh five 7:15 seven fifteen 7:30 seven thirty 7:45 seven forty-five 7:50 seven fifty Say the hour, then the minutes. 1–9 minutes take oh: 7:05 → seven oh five. o'clock /əˈklɒk/ goes only with full hours: seven o'clock. Past and to Time Said 3:05 five past three 3:15 (a) quarter past three 3:20 twenty past three 3:30 half past three 3:40 twenty to four 3:45 (a) quarter to four 3:55 five to four Minutes 1–30: past the hour. Minutes 31–59: to the next hour. Say the minutes first, then the hour: twenty to four. Minutes that are not 5, 10, 15… add minutes: three minutes past six. after for past, of for to: a quarter after three, ten of four. Parts of the day Time Said 07:00 seven a.m. / seven in the morning 12:00 midday / twelve noon 15:00 three p.m. / three in the afternoon 20:00 eight p.m. / eight in the evening 23:00 eleven p.m. / eleven at night 00:00 midnight a.m. = from midnight to midday; p.m. = from midday to midnight. In speech, the 12-hour clock is usual. Timetables use 24 hours: 19:30 = nineteen thirty. Approximate times Time Said Meaning 3:28 about half past three close to the time 3:57 nearly four a little before the time 2:03 just gone two (US: a little after two) a little after the time 5:02 just after five a little after the time 11:55 round about noon close to the time 7:00 seven o'clock on the dot exactly 9:00 nine sharp exactly Words such as about and nearly come before the time; on the dot and sharp come after it. Informal and formal clock talk Style Say Example Informal British half and the hour mean half past that hour 7:30 → half seven (US: seven thirty) Timetable the hour and the minutes as two numbers; 1–9 minutes take oh 14:05 → fourteen oh five Four digits hundred stands for a full hour; hours may follow 0700 → oh seven hundred / 2000 → twenty hundred hours Durations Use Rule Example How long for names the length of time We waited for two hours. Time needed takes names the time a job needs It takes ten minutes to walk there. Parts of an hour half takes no of; quarters take of half an hour / three quarters of an hour / an hour and a half Time ahead in looks ahead from now; the plural minutes takes an apostrophe before time See you in ten minutes' time. Time zones Use Rule Example Zone names GMT is UK winter time; BST is summer time, one hour ahead GMT → Greenwich Mean Time / BST → British Summer Time Offsets UTC plus or minus a number of hours gives the zone UTC+1 → UTC plus one Time in a place in and the place name the time there It is noon in New York when it is five in the afternoon in London. Ahead and behind ahead of means later; behind means earlier Paris is an hour ahead of London. / New York is five hours behind London. See you in ten minutes' time. the possessive plural takes an apostrophe

fixture.body: Be needs no helper and the subject is always in the sentence: Are you a student? / It is cold. Tense Future Will I be late? I will be late. I won't be late. Future Will you be late? You will be late. You won't be late. Future Will he be late? He will be late. He won't be late. Future Will she be late? She will be late. She won't be late. Future Will it be late? It will be late. It won't be late. Future Will we be late? We will be late. We won't be late. Future Will they be late? They will be late. They won't be late. Present Am I late? I am late. I am not late. Present Are you late? You are late. You aren't late. Present Is he late? He is late. He isn't late. Present Is she late? She is late. She isn't late. Present Is it late? It is late. It isn't late. Present Are we late? We are late. We aren't late. Present Are they late? They are late. They aren't late. Past Was I late? I was late. I wasn't late. Past Were you late? You were late. You weren't late. Past Was he late? He was late. He wasn't late. Past Was she late? She was late. She wasn't late. Past Was it late? It was late. It wasn't late. Past Were we late? We were late. We weren't late. Past Were they late? They were late. They weren't late. Overview be has its own form in each tense: will be for the future, am / is / are for the present, was / were for the past. be needs no helper: in questions it goes before the subject, in negatives it takes not. Present and past forms change with the person; will be is the same for everyone. you takes are and were, for one person and for many. Present: short forms Subject Full form Short form I I am a student. I'm a student. you You are late. You're late. he He is at home. He's at home. she She is happy. She's happy. it It is cold. It's cold. we We are friends. We're friends. they They are teachers. They're teachers. Speech and messages use the short forms. Negatives: isn't and aren't are usual; I'm not is the only short form with I. A noun subject takes is (singular) or are (plural): My parents are doctors. Present: questions and short answers Form Example be + subject Are you a student? wh-word + be + subject Where are you from? wh-word + be + subject What is your name? wh-word + be + subject How old are you? wh-word + be + subject How are you? A short answer repeats be; the positive answer takes the full form: Are you tired? — Yes, I am. / No, I'm not. Past: was and were Form I / he / she / it you / we / they + I was at home. We were at home. − She wasn't at home. They weren't at home. ? Was he at home? Were you at home? A short answer repeats was / were: Were you there? — Yes, I was. / No, I wasn't. Birth takes was / were born: I was born in 1995. Time words: yesterday, last night, last week, in 2010. Future: will be Use Example A future state or place I'll be at home tomorrow. Predictions It will be sunny at the weekend. Questions about the future Will you be there? Short forms: I'll be, she'll be, won't be. More about will: Simple Tenses. Use Use Example Name My name is Anna. Age I'm 20. / He is 30 years old. Nationality and origin She's Spanish. / We're from Madrid. Job He's a teacher. Description The house is big. Feelings and states I'm hungry. / They're tired. Place The keys are on the table. Weather, time, dates It's sunny. / It's 5 o'clock. A job takes a / an: He is a teacher. See Articles. Weather and time use the subject it: It is cold. For there is, see There is / there are. Typical errors Do you be a student? Are you a student? be makes questions by itself She are happy. She is happy. he / she / it → is We was at home. We were at home. you / we / they → were Did you be at home? Were you at home? be makes past questions by itself I will at home tomorrow. I will be at home tomorrow. will + be

fixture.body: Past simple and past participle are separate forms for many verbs: I went there. / I have gone there. Pattern Base form Past simple Past participle All three forms are the same put put put -ought / -aught buy bought bought Past and participle end in -d make made made Final -d becomes -t build built built Long vowel shortens, -t added keep kept kept /iː/ shortens to /e/ meet met met Vowel changes, past = participle sit sat sat Participle = base form come came come i → a → u drink drank drunk Participle in -en take took taken participle in -n / -ne go went gone Use finished actions: I went to Madrid. after have: I have gone there. Two accepted forms learn learnt / learned learnt / learned Confusing pairs lie / lay lay / laid lain / laid A compound takes the forms of its base verb undertake undertook undertaken Less frequent verbs follow the same patterns weave wove woven An old participle survives as an adjective sink sank sunk / sunken Overview The past simple is used for finished actions. See Past Simple. The past participle is used after have in the present perfect. See Present Perfect. Regular verbs add -ed to both forms: work – worked – worked. The Level column shows when a verb is usually met: A1 first, C2 last. Pattern: all three forms are the same Base form Past simple Past participle put put put cut cut cut let let let hit hit hit shut shut shut hurt hurt hurt cost cost cost set set set spread spread spread bet bet bet burst burst burst cast cast cast quit quit quit shed shed shed split split split thrust thrust thrust The three forms are the same. The sentence shows the tense: I put it there. / I have put it there. Pattern: past and participle in -ought / -aught Base form Past simple Past participle buy bought bought think thought thought bring brought brought catch caught caught teach taught taught fight fought fought Past and participle share one form. -ought and -aught are both pronounced /ɔːt/: bought /bɔːt/, caught /kɔːt/. Pattern: past and participle end in -d Base form Past simple Past participle have had had make made made say said /sed/ said /sed/ tell told told pay paid paid sell sold sold hear heard /hɜːd/ heard /hɜːd/ lay laid laid Past and participle share one form with -d at the end. The vowel or the stem changes in some verbs. say and hear change their vowel sound: say /seɪ/ → said /sed/, hear /hɪə/ → heard /hɜːd/. Pattern: final -d becomes -t Base form Past simple Past participle send sent sent spend spent spent build built built lend lent lent bend bent bent The final -d of the base verb changes to -t. Past and participle share one form. Pattern: the long vowel shortens and -t is added Base form Past simple Past participle feel felt felt keep kept kept sleep slept slept leave left left lose lost lost deal dealt /delt/ dealt /delt/ mean meant /ment/ meant /ment/ creep crept crept weep wept wept sweep swept swept The vowel is short in the past and the participle, and the form ends in -t: keep /kiːp/ → kept /kept/. leave → left and lose → lost change the final consonant as well: /liːv/ → /left/, /luːz/ → /lɒst/. Pattern: the vowel /iː/ shortens to /e/ Base form Past simple Past participle meet met met read read /red/ read /red/ lead led led feed fed fed flee fled fled bleed bled bled breed bred bred speed sped sped Past and participle share one form with the short vowel /e/: meet /miːt/ → met /met/. read is spelled the same in all three forms: /riːd/ in the base, /red/ in the past and the participle. Pattern: the vowel changes, past = participle Base form Past simple Past participle sit sat sat get got got find found found stand stood stood win won won understand understood understood hold held held shoot shot shot light lit lit dig dug dug hang hung hung stick stuck stuck strike struck struck swing swung swung spin spun spun bind bound bound grind ground ground wring wrung wrung shine shone /ʃɒn/ (US: /ʃoʊn/) shone /ʃɒn/ (US: /ʃoʊn/) sting stung stung cling clung clung fling flung flung A new vowel appears in the past simple, and the participle repeats it. the participle of get is gotten: I've gotten a new phone. British English keeps got. shine has shone for light and shined when it takes an object. The sun shone. / He shined his shoes. Pattern: participle = base form Base form Past simple Past participle come came come run ran run become became become overcome overcame overcome The participle equals the base verb. Only the past simple has its own form. Pattern: i → a → u Base form Past simple Past participle drink drank drunk begin began begun swim swam swum sing sang sung ring rang rung shrink shrank shrunk sink sank sunk spring sprang sprung stink stank stunk The vowel runs i → a → u: the past takes a, the participle takes u. Pattern: participle in -en Base form Past simple Past participle give gave given take took taken eat ate /et/ or /eɪt/ eaten write wrote written drive drove driven ride rode ridden break broke broken speak spoke spoken choose chose chosen forget forgot forgotten fall fell fallen wake woke woken steal stole stolen hide hid hidden freeze froze frozen arise arose arisen bite bit bitten beat beat beaten forbid forbade /fəˈbæd/ forbidden forgive forgave forgiven shake shook shaken rise rose risen prove proved proven / proved mistake mistook mistaken undertake undertook undertaken awake awoke awoken sow sowed sown tread trod trodden weave wove woven forsake forsook forsaken bear bore borne / born The past has its own vowel. The participle ends in -en. ate is /eɪt/. British English also uses /et/. born is only for birth. borne is for carrying and bearing. He was born in May. / She has borne the cost. Pattern: past in -ew, participle in -n Base form Past simple Past participle know knew known fly flew flown grow grew grown draw drew drawn throw threw thrown blow blew blown withdraw withdrew withdrawn The past ends in -ew and the participle ends in -n: know → knew → known. Pattern: participle in -n / -ne, past has its own form Base form Past simple Past participle be was / were been /biːn/ do did done /dʌn/ go went gone /ɡɒn/ see saw seen wear wore worn tear tore torn swear swore sworn undergo underwent undergone forgo forwent forgone outdo outdid outdone The participle ends in -n or -ne. The past is a form of its own. been is /biːn/ (US: /bɪn/). go has two participles: gone and been. gone = he is away. been = he went and came back: He has been to Paris. Two accepted forms Base form First form Second form learn learnt learned burn burnt burned dream dreamt /dremt/ dreamed /driːmd/ spell spelt spelled kneel knelt kneeled get got (US: gotten) dive dived (US: dove) sneak sneaked (US: snuck) dwell dwelt dwelled Both forms are correct. British English often uses the -t form; US English prefers -ed. Confusing pairs First verb Second verb lie, lay, lain: to rest, with no object lay, laid, laid: to put something down He has lain on the sofa all day. She laid the keys on the table. lie, lied, lied: to say what is not true He lied about his age. rise, rose, risen: to go up, with no object raise, raised, raised: to lift something The sun rose at six. They raised the price. sit, sat, sat: to take a seat set, set, set: to put or to prepare She sat by the window. He set the table. hang, hung, hung: to fix something up hang, hanged, hanged: to execute a person I hung the picture on the wall. The man was hanged for murder. find, found, found: to discover found, founded, founded: to set up an organisation I found my keys. She founded the company in 1990. wind /waɪnd/, wound /waʊnd/, wound: to turn or twist wound /wuːnd/, wounded, wounded: to injure She wound /waʊnd/ the clock. The knife wounded him. Compounds follow their base Verb Built on Past simple and participle understand stand understood withstand stand withstood mislead lead misled overtake take overtook, overtaken undertake take undertook, undertaken outgrow grow outgrew, outgrown rewrite write rewrote, rewritten foresee see foresaw, foreseen A compound takes the forms of the verb it contains. They have overtaken us. Old participles as adjectives Verb form Adjective He has drunk too much. a drunken brawl The ship has sunk. a sunken ship The jumper has shrunk. a shrunken head It has proved useful. a proven method The ice has melted. molten lead She was bound by the contract. our bounden duty She has learned /lɜːnd/ the rule. a learned /ˈlɜːnɪd/ scholar The priest blessed /blest/ the bread. the blessed /ˈblesɪd/ day She loved him. my beloved /bɪˈlʌvɪd/ wife After be, drunk is the usual adjective. drunken stands before a noun. Literary and archaic forms Base form Past simple Past participle Modern English clothe clad clad clothed work wrought wrought worked beget begot begotten fathered bid bade /bæd/ bidden told slay slew slain killed smite smote smitten struck spin span / spun spun spun spit spat / spit spat / spit spat These forms appear in old stories, poems and set phrases such as wrought iron and clad in black. Typical errors I goed to Madrid. I went to Madrid. irregular verbs have their own past form, no -ed She buyed a car. She bought a car. buy → bought I have went there. I have gone there. after have use the participle: gone I have saw it. I have seen it. after have use the participle: seen I seen him yesterday. I saw him yesterday. the past simple takes the past form: saw I have wrote a letter. I have written a letter. write → wrote → written He readed the book. He read /red/ the book. read is spelled the same in all forms, the past sounds /red/ She layed the table. She laid the table. lay → laid The price has rose. The price has risen. rise → rose → risen I hanged the picture on the wall. I hung the picture on the wall. hanged is only for execution

Point Rule Example Narrative present jokes, headlines, plot summaries, commentary, reporting verbs A man walks into a pub. Historic present a vivid shift to the present inside a past account Suddenly the door opens. Distance and politeness the past simple softens a request or a question about now Did you want to see me? Performative verbs saying the verb does the act I promise to be on time. Overview Each simple tense has a helper verb: will for the future, do / does for the present, did for the past. In questions the helper goes before the subject; in negatives it takes not: don't, doesn't, didn't, won't. After every helper the main verb is in the base form: Does she work? / She didn't work. Present and past statements have no helper: the verb itself takes -s (he, she, it) or -ed. will and did are the same for every person; only the present changes with he, she, it. be has its own forms: am / is / are, was / were. See To be. Present simple: form Subject Verb Example I / you / we / they V I live in Madrid. he / she / it V-s She lives in Madrid. singular noun V-s My brother lives in Madrid. plural noun V My parents live in Madrid. A short answer repeats the helper: Do you like tea? — Yes, I do. / No, I don't. A wh-word goes first: wh-word + do / does + subject + verb. Where does he live? When who or what is the subject, the verb follows directly, with -s: Who lives here? More question patterns: Questions and negatives. Present simple: the -s ending Verb ending Spelling Examples most verbs + s work → works / read → reads -s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x, -z + es pass → passes / wash → washes / watch → watches / fix → fixes -o + es go → goes / do → does consonant + y y → ies study → studies / try → tries vowel + y + s play → plays / buy → buys have own form have → has Sound After Examples /s/ voiceless sounds /p t k f θ/ stops /stɒps/ · works /wɜːks/ · laughs /lɑːfs/ /z/ voiced sounds and vowels lives /lɪvz/ · plays /pleɪz/ · goes /ɡəʊz/ /ɪz/ /s z ʃ tʃ dʒ/ washes /ˈwɒʃɪz/ · watches /ˈwɒtʃɪz/ · uses /ˈjuːzɪz/ Three verbs change their vowel sound: does /dʌz/, says /sez/, has /hæz/. Present simple: use Use Example Habits and routines I get up at 7. Facts and general truths Water boils at 100 °C. Permanent states She lives in London. Likes, dislikes, opinions I like coffee. / I think so. Jobs and regular activities He teaches maths. Timetables and schedules (future) The train leaves at 6:15. Instructions and directions You turn left at the bank. Performative verbs: saying the verb does the act I promise to be on time. / I apologise (US: apologize) for the delay. Formal declarations and suggestions I declare the meeting open. / I suggest we start again. Frequency adverbs go before the main verb and after be: I often walk to work. / She is always late. Time expressions go at the end: I swim every day. / She works late on Mondays. Verbs for states take the present simple, also for now: I know the answer. / I want a coffee. All frequency adverbs: Adverbs of frequency and manner. Present simple for narration and reporting Use Example Jokes and anecdotes A man walks into a pub and orders a drink. News headlines Government announces new law Plot summaries In the film, a young woman travels to Paris and falls in love. Sports commentary Smith passes to Jones, and Jones shoots! Reporting verbs: hear, gather, say I gather the meeting has moved. / They say it will rain. / It says here that the shop closes at six. Past simple: form be has its own past, with no helper: was / were. See To be. I was at home. / Were you there? Every other verb has one past form for every person: Verb type Form Example regular V-ed I watched TV. irregular own form I saw a film. A short answer repeats the helper: Did you like it? — Yes, I did. / No, I didn't. A wh-word goes first: wh-word + did + subject + verb. Where did they go? When who or what is the subject, the verb is in the past directly: Who called you? / What happened? Past simple: the -ed ending Verb ending Spelling Examples most verbs + ed work → worked / watch → watched / visit → visited -e + d live → lived / like → liked / arrive → arrived consonant + y y → ied study → studied / try → tried vowel + y + ed play → played / stay → stayed 1 vowel + 1 consonant, one syllable double the consonant + ed stop → stopped / plan → planned Sound After Examples /t/ voiceless sounds /p k f s ʃ tʃ θ/ stopped /stɒpt/ · worked /wɜːkt/ · watched /wɒtʃt/ /d/ voiced sounds and vowels lived /lɪvd/ · played /pleɪd/ · opened /ˈəʊpənd/ /ɪd/ /t d/ wanted /ˈwɒntɪd/ · needed /ˈniːdɪd/ · visited /ˈvɪzɪtɪd/ The ending adds a syllable only after /t/ and /d/: wanted has two syllables, worked has one. Past simple: irregular verbs Base verb Past simple Example go went We went home. have had I had lunch. do did She did her homework. see saw I saw Tom. get got He got a letter. make made They made a cake. take took I took a taxi. come came She came late. eat ate We ate pizza. buy bought I bought a coat. say said He said hello. write wrote I wrote an email. The irregular form is only for statements; questions and negatives take did + base verb: Did you go? More verbs: Irregular verbs table. Past simple: use Use Example Finished actions at a stated past time I visited Paris last year. Past states She was ill on Monday. Sequences of events I got up, had a shower and left. Past habits that are over When I was a child, I played outside every day. Time words: yesterday, last week, in 2020, two years ago. ago comes after the period: She left two days ago. Past habits also take used to: see Used to. Future simple: form Form Structure Example + will / 'll + V I'll help you. − will not / won't + V He won't come. ? will + subject + V Will she come? Short answer Yes, I will. / No, I won't. Will you call? — Yes, I will. Speech and messages use 'll and won't: 'll is /l/ after a vowel, /əl/ after a consonant; won't is /wəʊnt/. Future simple: use Use Example Decision at the moment of speaking It's cold. I'll close the window. Offers I'll carry your bag. Promises I won't tell anyone. Opinions and predictions (I think) I think she'll win. probably goes after will and before won't: It will probably rain. / It probably won't rain. Plans and arrangements take going to or the present continuous: see Future forms. Historic present Use Example A vivid moment inside an account in the past We were driving home when suddenly a deer jumps out. History writing and documentaries In 1789 the people of Paris storm the Bastille. Earlier events keep a past form He opens the letter. His brother had written it years ago. A shift to the present marks the peak of the story; suddenly and then often introduce it. Past simple for distance and politeness Use Example A polite question about what someone wants now Did you want to see me? A polite request I wondered if you could help me. A softened statement I just wanted to say thank you. A tentative suggestion I thought you might like it. The past form talks about now; the step back in time makes the sentence less direct. Compare: past, present and future Past simple Present simple Future simple did do / does will yesterday, last week, ago every day, usually, on Mondays tomorrow, next week, soon I worked yesterday. I work every day. I'll work tomorrow. Did she call? Does she call? Will she call? He didn't come. He doesn't come. He won't come. a story told as past events the same story told as if it happens now A man walked into a pub. A man walks into a pub. Typical errors She work here. She works here. he / she / it → V-s He doesn't works. He doesn't work. helper + base verb Where you live? Where do you live? questions need a helper Did you went there? Did you go there? did + base verb She didn't called. She didn't call. didn't + base verb I goed home. I went home. go → went (irregular verb) Did he was late? Was he late? be makes questions by itself He will goes. He will go. will + base verb Do you will come? Will you come? will makes questions by itself

Point Rule Example Result or duration perfect simple: a result or a number; continuous: a process or its length I've written five emails. / I've been writing all morning. First time and superlatives present perfect after it's the first time and after a superlative with ever It's the first time I've flown. Completed by a future time future perfect, with by or by the time By Friday I'll have finished. News and details the present perfect announces; the past simple gives the details The minister has resigned. He said the pressure was too great. Trap verbs of state take the simple perfect I've known her for years. Overview Each perfect tense is have + past participle: have / has for the present, had for the past. In questions the helper goes before the subject; in negatives it takes not: haven't, hasn't, hadn't. The main verb is always the past participle: worked, seen, gone. has goes with he, she, it; had is the same for everyone. Short forms: I've, she's (= she has), I'd (= I had). The past participle Type Rule Examples regular verbs V + -ed work → worked / live → lived / study → studied irregular, same as past simple participle = past simple form have → had / buy → bought / meet → met irregular, own form learn each one see → seen / write → written / eat → eaten / do → done go, be go has two participles go → gone / been · be → been The -ed spelling is the same as in the past simple: see Simple Tenses. All irregular forms: Irregular verbs table. Present perfect: form A short answer repeats have / has: Have you met Tom? — Yes, I have. / No, I haven't. ever, never, just and already go between have / has and the participle: I've never seen snow. / He's just left. yet goes at the end, in negatives and questions: I haven't finished yet. / Have you finished yet? How long asks about the length of a state up to now: How long have you lived here? Present perfect: use Use Example Life experience, no time given I've been to Paris twice. Recent news I've just seen Anna. Result visible now I've lost my keys. Unfinished time (today, this week) I've had three coffees today. A state from the past up to now (for, since) She's lived here since 2019. The first or second time something happens It's the first time (that) I've flown. A superlative with ever This is the best film I've ever seen. Since with a clause in the past simple Ihaven't smoked since I left school. How long it is since something happened It's been two years since we last met. Time up to now: so far, lately, recently, in the last few days She's called three times so far. / I've been busy in the last few days. The present perfect announces news and the past simple gives the details The minister has resigned. He said the pressure was too great. A general statement about history up to now Humans have always looked up at the stars. been = went and came back; gone = went and is still there: She's been to Spain. / She's gone to Spain. for takes a length of time; since takes a starting point: I've known her for ten years / since 2015. Present perfect continuous: form Subject Form Example I / you / we / they have / 've + been + V-ing I've been waiting for an hour. he / she / it has / 's + been + V-ing She's been working all day. singular noun has been + V-ing The baby has been sleeping since two. The negative is haven't been / hasn't been and the -ing verb: She hasn't been feeling well. A question starts with Have / Has; the short answer repeats it: Have you been waiting long? — Yes, I have. / No, I haven't. Verbs of state take the simple perfect, also for duration: I've known her for years. Present perfect continuous: use Use Example An activity that began in the past and is still going I've been studying since nine. An activity that has just stopped, with a result you can see You look wet. — I've been walking in the rain. Duration: how long, for, since How long have you been waiting? / She's been learning Greek for two years. A repeated activity in recent time He's been going to the gym a lot lately. Past perfect: form A short answer repeats had: Had they left? — Yes, they had. / No, they hadn't. already, just and never go between had and the participle: I'd never flown before. Past perfect: use Use Example An action before another past action When I got home, she had already cooked. An action before a past time By 8 o'clock he had left. The reason for a past situation He was tired. He had worked all night. Time words: when, after, before, by the time, already. The story itself takes the past simple; the past perfect looks back from it. Past perfect continuous: form and use Use Example Duration before a past moment By noon they had been walking for four hours. The cause of a past situation She was tired because she had been working all night. The form is had been + V-ing for every person; the negative is hadn't been. We hadn't been waiting long. A question starts with Had; the short answer repeats it: Had they been waiting long? — Yes, they had. / No, they hadn't. Future perfect: form and use Use Example Completed before a future time By Friday I'll have finished the report. Completed before another future event By the time you arrive, we'll have eaten. The form is will have + past participle for every person; the negative is won't have. She won't have arrived by six. A question starts with Will; the short answer repeats it: Will you have finished by six? — Yes, I will. / No, I won't. Time words: by, by then, by the time, before. I'll have left before you wake up. Future perfect continuous: form and use Use Example Duration up to a future time By June I'll have been working here for ten years. An activity that fills the time before a future moment When you arrive, I'll have been cooking all afternoon. The form is will have been + V-ing for every person; the negative is won't have been. He won't have been sleeping long. A question starts with Will: Will you have been waiting long? Compare: present perfect and past simple Present perfect Past simple past event, time open or unfinished finished time, stated or known I've seen that film. I saw it last night. ever, never, just, already, yet yesterday, last week, ago Have you eaten yet? (US: Did you eat yet?) A finished-time word (yesterday, last week, ago) takes the past simple. the past simple is common with just, already and yet: I just ate. Compare: perfect simple and perfect continuous Perfect simple Perfect continuous a result or a number a process or its length I've written five emails. I've been writing emails all morning. the job is finished the activity counts; the job may not be finished I've painted the room. I've been painting the room. How many emails have you written? How long have you been writing? Typical errors I have seen him yesterday. I saw him yesterday. finished time → past simple I live here since 2010. I have lived here since 2010. since / for + state up to now → present perfect She has went home. She has gone home. have / has + past participle She have lost her keys. She has lost her keys. he / she / it → has I have gone to Paris twice. I have been to Paris twice. a visit and return → been When I arrived, the film has already started. When I arrived, the film had already started. earlier past action → had + participle Had you saw him? Had you seen him? after had use the past participle

fixture.body: Be and modals invert or take not; other verbs use do, does or did with the base verb: Do you like tea? Point Rule Example Negative: be, modals subject + be / modal + not They are not at home. / He can't drive. Question: be, modals be / modal + subject Are they at home? / Can he drive? Negative: other verbs subject + don't / doesn't / didn't + base verb He doesn't like jazz. Question: other verbs do / does / did + subject + base verb Did you call her? do, does, did I / you / we / they → do, he / she / it → does, past → did Do you like jazz? Wh-question wh-word + auxiliary + subject + base verb Where do you live? / Where are you from? Subject question no do / does / did; the verb takes the tense Who called you? Short answer repeat the be, modal or auxiliary verb Yes, she can. / No, she can't. Negative question helper + n't + subject; expects yes or shows surprise Isn't it lovely? / Haven't you finished? Fronted negative after not only / no sooner / nowhere the auxiliary comes first No sooner had we sat down than the phone rang. Understatement a negative with an opposite word states a fact mildly The plan is not without risk. Trap after do / does / did the verb is the base form Did you go? Overview be and modal verbs invert with the subject or take not. Other verbs use do / does / did. Every question and negative sentence has a subject. Form: be and modals Form Pattern Example Negative subject + be / modal + not They are not at home. / He can't drive. Question be / modal + subject Are they at home? / Can he drive? be and can, will, should, must need no do / does / did. am not has the short form I'm not: I'm not ready. have got inverts too: Have you got a pen? Form: do, does and did Auxiliary Subject and tense Example do / don't I / you / we / they, present Do you like jazz? does / doesn't he / she / it, present He doesn't like jazz. did / didn't every subject, past Did you call her? The negative order is subject + don't / doesn't / didn't + base verb: We didn't see him. The question order is do / does / did + subject + base verb: Does she work here? After do / does / did the verb is in the base form: Did you call? The auxiliary carries the tense and the person; the main verb stays unchanged. Present tables: Present Simple. Past: Past simple. A negative sentence takes one negative word: I don't know anything. / I know nothing. Form: negative contractions Full form Short form Example is not isn't It isn't cold. are not aren't They aren't here. was / were not wasn't / weren't We weren't late. do / does / did not don't / doesn't / didn't She doesn't know. cannot can't I can't see. will not won't It won't work. should / must / could / would not shouldn't / mustn't / couldn't / wouldn't You shouldn't go. Speech and messages use the short forms. The full forms add emphasis: I do not agree. Form: wh-questions Wh-word Asks about Example what a thing What do you want? where a place Where does he live? when a time When is the party? who a person Who did you meet? why a reason Why are you late? how a way How do you get to work? which a choice Which bag is yours? whose an owner Whose keys are these? how much an amount or a price How much is this? how many a number How many brothers have you got? how often frequency How often do you swim? how old age How old is your sister? how long a length of time How long is the film? The order is wh-word + auxiliary + subject + base verb: Where do you live? With be the order is wh-word + be + subject: Where are you from? which and whose can take a noun: Which colour do you like? how many takes a plural noun, how much an uncountable noun: How many eggs? / How much milk? Form: subject questions Question word Pattern Example who who + verb Who called you? what what + verb What happens next? which / how many which / how many + noun + verb How many people came? When the question word is the subject, the question has no do / does / did. The verb takes the tense directly: Who lives here? / Who lived here? Form: short answers Question Yes No Are you tired? Yes, I am. No, I'm not. Can she swim? Yes, she can. No, she can't. Did he call? Yes, he did. No, he didn't. A short answer repeats the be, modal or auxiliary verb from the question. A positive short answer keeps the full form: Yes, I am. For do / does see Present Simple. Pronunciation: question intonation Question Voice Example yes / no rises at the end Do you like tea? ↗ wh- falls at the end Where do you live? ↘ Form: negative questions Form Shows Example Isn't it …? expects the answer yes: a shared opinion Isn't it a lovely view? Haven't you …? surprise that something has not happened Haven't you finished yet? Don't you think …? asks for an opinion politely Don't you think it's too late? Why don't we …? a suggestion Why don't we eat out tonight? Aren't I …? the negative question for am Aren't I late? Is it not …? formal: the full form of not Is it not time to go? Yes answers a positive fact and no a negative fact, whatever the form of the question. Don't you like it? — No, I don't. Form: questions with prepositions Pattern Style Example wh-word + helper + subject + V + preposition everyday Who are you talking to? what + helper + subject + for everyday What is this button for? preposition + whom + helper + subject + V formal To whom are you speaking? A preposition at the front takes whom; everyday questions use who and leave the preposition at the end. With whom did you go? / Who did you go with? Form: emphatic wh-questions Form Shows Example wh-word + on earth / in the world strong surprise or annoyance What on earth are you doing? / Why in the world did you leave? wh-word + ever surprise How ever did you find us? / Who ever said that? subject + verb + wh-word an echo question: surprise, or a request to say it again I quit my job. — You did what? ↗ The emphatic phrase follows the wh-word, and the question keeps its usual word order. Where in the world did you put it? Form: more question types Form Use Example How come + clause asks the reason, with surprise; the clause keeps statement order How come you're late? What if + clause asks about a possibility or a risk What if it rains? What about / How about + noun / -ing a suggestion or an offer How about going for a walk? / What about Tom? Why not + V a suggestion Why not ask her? helper + subject + option + or + option a choice: the voice rises on the first option and falls on the last Is it red ↗or blue? ↘ wh-word + verb + wh-word asks about several parts at once Who said what to whom? / Who bought what? Polite and formal questions Form Use Example Might I ask …? a formal request for information Might I ask who is calling? Would you be so kind as to …? a formal request for action Would you be so kind as to close the window? Do you happen to know …? a tentative question: the speaker does not assume you know Do you happen to know where the station is? After these frames a wh-clause keeps statement order, with no inverted auxiliary. Might I ask what time the shop opens? Rhetorical and statement questions Question It means Example a statement with a rising voice a check, or surprise You're leaving? ↗ Who cares? nobody cares It's only a game. Who cares? Why bother? there is no reason to try It never works. Why bother? What difference does it make? it makes no difference We'll be late either way. What difference does it make? Negation: forms Word Rule Example no no before a noun means the same as not any We have no milk. / We haven't any milk. none a pronoun for a noun already named None of them came. / There was none left. neither not one of two things Neither of them called. not … either adds to a negative statement I don't like jazz either. nor / neither adds a negative to a negative; the auxiliary comes before the subject She can't swim, nor can he. / I don't know. Neither do I. not … at all stronger than not alone I didn't like it at all. not even includes even the smallest or the most expected thing He didn't even say hello. not … yet it has not happened so far She hasn't called yet. no longer / not any longer something was true before and is not true now He no longer lives here. / He doesn't live here any longer. hardly / scarcely / barely / seldom / rarely negative in meaning, so the verb stays positive I can hardly hear you. / She rarely complains. I don't think … the negative moves to the main verb, with think / believe / suppose / expect I don't think he'll come. ≠ I think he won't come. Form: negating non-finite verbs Form Use Example not + to + V after verbs that take the infinitive She told me not to worry. not + -ing after verbs that take -ing, and in a clause of reason I regret not telling you. / Not knowing the way, we asked. not having + past participle an earlier action as the reason Not having eaten all day, he was hungry. without + -ing the action that is left out She left without saying goodbye. Negation for focus Form Shows Example not … until only at that point, and not before She didn't arrive until noon. not only … but also adds a second point; at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject Not only did she win, she also set a record. no sooner … than one thing right after another; at the start, had comes before the subject No sooner had we sat down than the phone rang. nowhere no place at all; at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject Nowhere else is the air so clean. not a + noun none at all, stronger than not any He didn't say a word. / Not a soul was there. no + noun the opposite of the noun: no fool means clever He's no fool. / No idea. not nearly far less than It's not nearly as hot as yesterday. none too not at all, with a touch of irony She was none too pleased. not that says that a possible point does not matter He's late again. Not that I mind. Understatement by negation Phrase It means Example not bad quite good, sometimes very good The soup is not bad. not unlike similar to Her style is not unlike her mother's. not a little very I was not a little surprised. no small achievement a great achievement Finishing in a week was no small achievement. not without with some The plan is not without risk. not infrequently often Delays happen not infrequently. hardly unexpected quite expected The result was hardly unexpected. A negative joined to an opposite word states a fact mildly; the effect is formal or ironic. Scope of negation Word Some, not all None all Not all the guests came. None of the guests came. both Not both of them are right. Neither of them is right. always She is not always late. She is never late. everyone Not everyone agreed. No one agreed. In standard English two negatives cancel each other, and the sentence is positive. I can't not go. = I have to go. Emphasis adds a word such as at all / whatsoever to one negative. I have no time whatsoever. any / ever / at all need a negative setting: a negative, a question, an if clause or a comparison. Setting Example a negative She doesn't have any friends here. / It didn't help at all. a question Have you ever been to Rome? / Do you have any questions? an if clause If you ever need help, call me. a comparison She sings better than anyone I know. a word with a negative meaning She left without any money. / He hardly ever calls. Typical errors Did you went? Did you go? after did the verb is in the base form Who did call you? Who called you? a subject question has no did Do she like tea? Does she like tea? he / she / it → does To who are you speaking? To whom are you speaking? a preposition at the front takes whom How come did you leave? How come you left? how come keeps statement order I can't hardly hear you. I can hardly hear you. hardly is already negative: the verb stays positive Do you happen to know where is the station? Do you happen to know where the station is? the wh-clause keeps statement order Not only he forgot, he lost the keys. Not only did he forget, he lost the keys. after not only at the start the auxiliary comes before the subject

fixture.body: After if the verb is in the present simple, even for the future: If it rains / we'll stay in. Point Rule Example Zero: facts if + present, present If you mix blue and yellow, you get green. First: real possibilities if + present, will + V If you study, you'll pass. Second: unreal situations if + past simple, would + V If I won the lottery, I'd buy a house. Third: unreal past if + had + past participle, would have + past participle If I had known, I would have called. Mixed a past condition with a present result, or the reverse If I had taken the job, I would be rich now. The if-clause present simple, also for the future If it rains, we'll stay in. Order if-clause first: comma; if-clause second: no comma If it rains, we'll stay in. / We'll stay in if it rains. Other words for if as long as means only if; in case means as a precaution Take a coat in case it gets cold. Inversion Had, were or should first replaces if; formal Had I known, I would have called. Formal conditions in the event that, on the proviso that, were it not for Were it not for the noise, this would be a perfect house. Trap were for every person, also in advice If I were you, I'd take the train. Trap unless means if … not; the verb is affirmative Unless you hurry, you'll miss the bus. Overview Zero and first conditionals talk about real situations. The second talks about imagined ones. The third conditional imagines a past that did not happen. Mixed conditionals join a past and a present. Form: zero and first Type Pattern Example Zero if + present, present If you mix blue and yellow, you get green. First if + present, will + V If you study, you'll pass. First (negative) if + don't / doesn't + V, will + V If you don't hurry, you'll miss the bus. The if-clause uses the present simple, also for the future. The first conditional main clause can also use can, may or an imperative: If you feel ill, call me. Form: second Type Pattern Example Second if + past simple, would + V If I won the lottery, I'd buy a house. Second (negative) if + didn't + V, would + V If I didn't have to work, I'd travel. Second with be if + were, would + V If it were sunny, we'd go out. The past simple in the if-clause refers to the present or the future. were works for every person: If he were here, he'd help. was is common in informal speech. The main clause can also use could or might: If I had time, I could help. Form: third conditional Type Pattern Example Third if + had + past participle, would have + past participle If I had known, I would have called. Third (negative) if + hadn't + past participle, wouldn't have + past participle If she hadn't missed the bus, she wouldn't have been late. Third with could or might if + had + past participle, could / might + have + past participle If we had left earlier, we could have caught the train. Third (question) wh-word + would + subject + have + past participle? What would you have done if you had missed the flight? Third (continuous condition) if + had been + V-ing, would have + past participle If she had been watching the road, she would have seen the dog. Third (continuous result) if + had + past participle, would have been + V-ing If you hadn't phoned, I would have been waiting for hours. 'd stands for had in the if-clause and for would in the main clause: If I'd known, I'd have called. would have is spoken as would've /ˈwʊdəv/. Form: mixed conditionals Type Pattern Example Past condition, present result if + had + past participle, would + V If I had taken the job, I would be rich now. Present condition, past result if + past simple, would have + past participle If I were braver, I would have spoken up. now, still and today point to the present half; then and at the time point to the past half. If she had accepted the offer, she would still be living in Paris. could and might replace would in either half: If I had studied law, I could be a judge now. Order of the clauses Order Example if-clause first: comma If it rains, we'll stay in. if-clause second: no comma We'll stay in if it rains. Use Use Example Facts and general truths (zero) If you press this button, the door opens. Real possibilities in the future (first) If I see Ana, I'll tell her. Unreal or unlikely situations (second) If I were a bird, I'd fly to Spain. Advice: If I were you (second) If I were you, I'd take the train. Use Example Regret about the past (third) If I had saved more, I could have bought the house. Relief that something did not happen (third) If we had missed the last train, we would have been stuck. Unless unless means if … not. It takes an affirmative verb: Unless you hurry, you'll miss the bus. = If you don't hurry, you'll miss the bus. unless goes with the zero and first conditionals. See Conjunctions and Linkers. Other words for if Word Meaning Example as long as / so long as only if You can stay as long as you are quiet. provided (that) / providing (that) only if; a little more formal We'll start provided that everyone is here. on condition that only if; a term that has been agreed She agreed to talk on condition that her name stayed secret. supposing / assuming imagine that, or take as true Supposing you lost your passport, what would you do? / Assuming the shop is open, we can buy it today. even if the result is the same in any case I'll go even if it rains. only if and in no other case You can leave only if you have finished. in case as a precaution, because it may happen Take a coat in case it gets cold. otherwise / or else if not; the result of the opposite Hurry up. Otherwise, we'll miss the train. / Be quiet, or else you'll wake the baby. if only a strong wish or regret If only I had more time. / If only I had listened. if only for / if only to even if for this one reason alone Stay a little longer, if only for an hour. / Call her, if only to say sorry. as long as and provided that take a present form for the future. We'll stay as long as you need us. otherwise and or else start a new clause after a full stop, a semicolon or a comma. More on if only: Wishes and Unreal Tenses. Special if-clauses Pattern Meaning Example if + you + will / would + base verb polite request; would is more formal If you would follow me, I'll show you the room. / If you will wait here, the doctor will see you. if + subject + have / has + past participle an action finished before the main clause If you've finished, we can go. if + subject + am / is / are + V-ing an action in progress or a plan If you're going out, buy some milk. if adjective short for if it is possible, necessary and so on Call me back, if possible. / Bring a pen, if necessary. if so / if not refers back to the last statement or question Are you free tonight? If so, join us. / Is it raining? If not, let's walk. if any / if ever / if at all limits a claim: perhaps none, perhaps very few There are few mistakes, if any. / She rarely, if ever, complains. Inverted conditionals Pattern Replaces Example Had + subject + past participle if + subject + had + past participle Had I known, I would have called. Were + subject if + subject + were Were I you, I would wait. Should + subject + base verb if + subject + should + base verb Should you need help, call me. Had + subject + not + past participle if + subject + hadn't + past participle Had they not left early, they would have missed the train. had, were and should alone open an inverted conditional, and the clause drops if. Inverted conditionals belong to formal speech and writing. Had I known, I would have called. = If I had known, I would have called. If it weren't for, but for and without Phrase Meaning Example if it weren't for + noun present: without this cause or help If it weren't for the traffic, we would be there by now. if it hadn't been for + noun past: without this cause or help If it hadn't been for your map, we would have got lost. but for + noun formal: present or past But for the storm, we would have arrived on time. without + noun / V-ing if there were no, if you do not have Without a ticket, you can't get in. / Without your help, I would have failed. with + noun if there is, if we have With a bit of luck, we'll win. / With more time, I could do better. in the event of / in case of + noun if there is; notices and rules In the event of fire, use the stairs. / In case of fire, break the glass. given that + clause since this is so; a condition taken as a fact Given that it is late, we should go. Remote possibility: were to and should Pattern Meaning Example if + subject + were to + base verb an unlikely or purely imagined event If you were to win, what would you do? / If the plan were to fail, we would start again. if + subject + should + base verb an unlikely event; the main clause often gives an instruction If anyone should call, take a message. / If you should change your mind, tell me. were to and should make a condition sound unlikely and tentative. Formal and legal conditions Phrase Meaning Example in the event that + clause if this happens; notices and contracts In the event that you cannot attend, please tell us. on the proviso that + clause only if; a stated condition He lent the money on the proviso that it was repaid by May. on the understanding that + clause if it is agreed that You may use the room on the understanding that you leave it tidy. provided always that + clause legal: adds a limit to a rule The tenant may sublet, provided always that the owner agrees in writing. granted that + clause accepting a point before disagreeing Granted that the plan is risky, it may still work. in the event that takes a present form, or should for a remote case. In the event that it should rain, the match will move indoors. Inversion: were it not for, were it to Pattern Meaning Example Were it not for + noun formal: if it weren't for Were it not for the noise, this would be a perfect house. Had it not been for + noun formal: if it hadn't been for Had it not been for his advice, we would have failed. Were + subject + to + base verb formal: if it were to Were it to rain, the match would move indoors. Even were + subject + to + base verb concession: even if it were to Even were he to resign, the problem would remain. Compare: first and second conditional First conditional Second conditional real, possible imagined, unlikely If I win, I'll buy a car. If I won, I'd buy a car. If we have time, we'll visit you. If we had time, we'd visit you. The speaker chooses by how likely the situation seems. Compare: second and third conditional Second conditional Third conditional imagined present or future imagined past may still be true or happen too late to change If I had the money, I would buy it. If I had had the money, I would have bought it. If she studied harder, she would pass. If she had studied harder, she would have passed. Compare: if and in case If In case the main clause happens only when the condition is met the main clause happens first, as a precaution Put on a coat if it gets cold. Take a coat in case it gets cold. I'll call a taxi if the bus is late. I'll call a taxi in case the bus is late. Typical errors If I am you, I would go. If I were you, I'd go. advice uses If I were you If I win the lottery, I would buy a house. If I won the lottery, I would buy a house. match the pair: present + will or past + would If it rains we'll stay in. If it rains, we'll stay in. comma after an if-clause at the start Unless you don't hurry, you'll miss the bus. Unless you hurry, you'll miss the bus. unless already means if … not If she come, I'll call you. If she comes, I'll call you. she / he / it → V-s in the if-clause If I would have known, I would have called. If I had known, I would have called. the if-clause takes had + past participle I would of called. I would have called. would have is spoken would've; the verb is have In case you see Ana, say hello. If you see Ana, say hello. in case gives a reason for acting I'll come as long as it will stop raining. I'll come as long as it stops raining. as long as takes a present form for the future Hadn't I known, I would have called. Had I not known, I would have called. not follows the subject in an inverted conditional

fixture.body: Who, which and that replace the noun and the clause has no second pronoun: The woman who lives here is my aunt. Point Rule Example Form noun + who / which / that + clause; right after the noun The woman who lives next door is a nurse. who, which who for people, which for things The woman who lives next door is a nurse. / The book which I bought was cheap. that people or things, in defining clauses only The film that we saw was long. whose possession; a noun follows The man whose car was stolen called the police. where places The café where we met has closed. Subject pronoun stays: a verb follows The girl who speaks French is my cousin. Object pronoun can be left out in a defining clause only The film I saw was long. Defining says which one; no commas The man who called is my uncle. Non-defining extra information in commas; who / which / whose / where Paris, which I visited in May, is beautiful. Fronted preposition the preposition comes before whom / which; formal The woman to whom I spoke was kind. Infinitive clause noun + to + V; the preposition stays at the end I need someone to talk to. Formal relatives whereby / wherein / whereupon in formal and legal English They set up a system whereby tickets are sold online. Trap where already includes the preposition The house where I live is old. Form: relative pronouns Word Refers to Example who people The woman who lives next door is a nurse. which things The book which I bought was cheap. that people or things (defining clauses) The film that we saw was long. whose possession The man whose car was stolen called the police. where places The café where we met has closed. A relative clause comes straight after the noun it describes. whose is followed by a noun: whose car, whose idea. where includes the preposition: the house where I live. whom is the formal object form: The man whom I met. Everyday English uses who or no pronoun. Form: defining clauses A defining clause says which person or thing. It has no commas. The man who called is my uncle. The pronoun is With pronoun Without pronoun subject (verb follows) The girl who speaks French is my cousin. object (subject follows) The film that I saw was long. The film I saw was long. object of a preposition The man who I spoke to was kind. The man I spoke to was kind. A subject pronoun stays: who / which / that is followed by a verb. An object pronoun can be left out: who / which / that is followed by a subject. In everyday English the preposition goes to the end of the clause. Form: non-defining clauses A non-defining clause adds extra information. Commas separate it from the rest. My uncle, who lives in Leeds, is a doctor. Feature Defining Non-defining Information says which one extra, can be removed Commas none yes, and a pause in speech Pronouns who / which / that who / which / whose / where Leave out the object pronoun possible never Example Paris, which I visited in May, is beautiful. Tom, whose brother is a chef, cooks well. which can refer to a whole clause: He passed the exam, which surprised everyone. Form: preposition and relative pronoun Pattern Refers to Example preposition + whom people The woman to whom I spoke was kind. / The friends with whom I travelled live in Spain. preposition + which things The house in which he lives is old. / The pen with which she signed was gold. Only whom and which can follow a preposition at the front; this order is formal. She has a car of which she is proud. Form: quantifier and whom or which Pattern Refers to Example some / many / all / none / both / neither / the majority + of + whom people The guests, some of whom had travelled far, were tired. / She has two sons, both of whom live abroad. some / many / all / none / both / neither / the majority + of + which things I bought two books, neither of which was cheap. / The shops, many of which were closed, looked empty. These clauses are non-defining, so a comma comes before the quantifier. He has three cars, all of which are red. Form: when, where, why and the way Word After Example when a time noun: day, year, moment I remember the day (when) we met. where a place, or a case, situation or point There are cases where this fails. why the noun reason That is the reason (why) he left. the way how something is done I like the way (in which) she explains things. After a time noun or reason, that can replace when and why. That was the year that she moved. Form: that after all, only and superlatives After Pronoun Example all / everything / nothing / something / little / much that Everything that she said was true. / All that I know is this. only / first / last / a superlative that It is the only book that I own. / It is the best film that I have seen. In these clauses that is usual and which is rare. Form: which for a whole clause Form Use Example which is why the first clause is the reason for the second She was ill, which is why she stayed home. in which case if the first clause is true It may rain, in which case we'll stay in. which means the result of the first clause The shop is closed, which means we can't buy it. Form: reduced relative clauses Form Replaces Example noun + -ing an active clause: who is standing, who stands The man standing at the door is my uncle. = The man who is standing at the door is my uncle. noun + past participle a passive clause: which was written, that is made The book written by Orwell is on the shelf. = The book which was written by Orwell is on the shelf. noun + to + V a clause after first, last, only or a superlative She was the first to arrive. / This is the best way to do it. noun + adjective who is, who are The people present were happy. = The people who were present were happy. noun + preposition + noun who has, who wears, which is The girl with the red hat is my sister. = The girl who is wearing the red hat is my sister. A reduced clause leaves out the relative pronoun and the verb be. Form: as as a relative pronoun Form Use Example as + clause comments on the whole main clause, after it or before it He was late, as is often the case. / As we have seen, the plan failed. such + noun + as things of the kind that follows He lent me such books as he had. the same + noun + as identical or very similar She has the same bag as I have. as many + noun + as an amount equal to the need Take as many books as you need. Form: relative clauses with infinitives Form Use Example noun + to + V + preposition the noun is the object of the preposition I need a place to live in. / I need someone to talk to. noun + to + V the person or thing that the infinitive is about She is the best person to ask. noun + subject + V + preposition the preposition stays at the end of the clause That is the person I'm waiting for. noun + subject + phrasal verb a phrasal verb keeps its particle and preposition together This is the plan we came up with. Form: extraposed relative clauses Form Use Example after a short verb the clause is long, so it moves to the end A man came in who looked ill. after a passive verb the clause adds news about a new thing A book has been published which explains this. after the noun time formal: the clause names the time The time has come when we must act. The relative clause moves to the end when the rest of the sentence is short. Form: those who and anyone who Form Refers to Example those who people in general, plural Those who work hard usually succeed. anyone who / everyone who / someone who a person or people with this quality Anyone who wants to join should sign here. / Everyone who came enjoyed it. all who every person in a group, in formal style All who enter must sign in. he who anyone, in proverbs and old style He who hesitates is lost. Punctuation: non-defining clauses Mark Use Example commas a pair around a clause in the middle of the sentence My sister, who lives in Leeds, is a nurse. commas one comma before a clause at the end I called my sister, who lives in Leeds. dashes a stronger break, in informal or dramatic writing My sister – who lives in Leeds – is a nurse. Formal relative adverbs Form Means Example whereby by which They set up a system whereby tickets are sold online. wherein in which The report, wherein the terms are set out, is online. whereupon after which, and then He objected, whereupon she left. thereof of it or of that; formal and legal The terms thereof are set out below. in respect of which concerning It is a sum in respect of which tax is due. the extent to which how far We discussed the extent to which they cooperate. the basis on which the grounds of a decision They explained the basis on which the prize is awarded. the manner in which the way something is done I admired the manner in which she handled it. Form: whose and of which Form Use Example whose + noun people and things; the usual choice A company whose founder left is struggling. the + noun + of which things; formal, in a non-defining clause The company, the founder of which left, is struggling. preposition + whose + noun formal: the preposition stands first She is the woman in whose house we stayed. Form: hypothetical antecedents Form Use Example noun + who + would + V a person who is imagined or typical, and not a known one I need a friend who would tell me the truth. noun + that + past a wished-for thing, with the past tense of an unreal condition I'd like a job that paid more. noun + that + were formal: the subjunctive were I wish I had a house that were nearer the sea. Typical errors The man which lives next door is a doctor. The man who lives next door is a doctor. people → who or that The house where I live in is old. The house where I live is old. / The house I live in is old. where includes the preposition My uncle, that lives in Leeds, is a doctor. My uncle, who lives in Leeds, is a doctor. non-defining clauses use who or which The film that I saw it was long. The film that I saw was long. the pronoun stands for the object I know a man lives in Paris. I know a man who lives in Paris. a subject pronoun stays Paris, which I visited it in May, is beautiful. Paris, which I visited in May, is beautiful. which stands for the object Paris which I visited in May is beautiful. Paris, which I visited in May, is beautiful. non-defining clauses need commas The woman to who I spoke was kind. The woman to whom I spoke was kind. a preposition at the front takes whom I like the way how she explains things. I like the way she explains things. the way takes a clause directly, or in which She has two sons, both of them live abroad. fixture.body: Be changes with the tense and the participle stays: English is spoken here. Point Rule Example Form the object becomes the subject; be + past participle Shakespeare wrote Hamlet. → Hamlet was written by Shakespeare. Present simple am / is / are + V-ed English is spoken here. Past simple was / were + V-ed The bridge was built in 1990. Present perfect has / have been + V-ed The window has been broken. will, can, must will / can / must be + V-ed The results will be sent tomorrow. Negative, question negative: be + not + V-ed; question: be + subject + V-ed The room wasn't cleaned. / Was the room cleaned? Use unknown or unimportant doer, processes, news, formal writing My phone was stolen on the train. / Wine is made from grapes. by / with by names a new or important doer; with names a tool The song was written by Adele. Other forms modal be + V-ed; continuous being + V-ed The form must be signed. / The road is being repaired. Reporting passive subject + be said + to + base verb reports opinions He is said to be rich. Formal writing the agentless passive reports method and findings The samples were heated to 80 degrees. Middle voice an active verb with a passive meaning This book reads well. Trap verbs without an object stay active: happen / arrive / die The accident happened yesterday. Trap use the past participle: made, written, sold, taken The window was broken. Form: active to passive Active Passive Shakespeare wrote Hamlet. Hamlet was written by Shakespeare. They sell tickets online. Tickets are sold online. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive. The verb is be in the tense of the active verb, plus the past participle. Verbs with an object have a passive. happen, arrive, die and sleep have an active form only. Form: tenses Tense Form Example Present simple am / is / are + V-ed English is spoken here. Past simple was / were + V-ed The bridge was built in 1990. Present perfect has / have been + V-ed The window has been broken. will will be + V-ed The results will be sent tomorrow. can / must can / must be + V-ed The door must be locked. V-ed = past participle: made, written, sold, taken, built. Irregular participles are in the irregular verbs table. Form: modals and perfect modals Type Form Example Modal must / should / ought to / may / might / could / can't + be + V-ed The work must be done today. / Children should be told the truth. / Some mistakes can't be avoided. Modal perfect should / could / might / must / can't + have been + V-ed You should have been told. / The accident could have been avoided. More on the modal perfect: Modal Verbs in the Past: must have, should have. Form: continuous and perfect passives Form Pattern Example Present continuous am / is / are + being + V-ed The road is being repaired. Past continuous was / were + being + V-ed The bridge was being built when I arrived. Past perfect had been + V-ed The house had been sold before we called. Future perfect will have been + V-ed The work will have been finished by Friday. Passive gerund being + V-ed She hates being told what to do. Passive infinitive to be + V-ed I want to be told the truth. Perfect passive infinitive to have been + V-ed He was glad to have been chosen. Form: negatives and questions Type Pattern Example Negative be + not + V-ed The room wasn't cleaned. Question be + subject + V-ed Was the room cleaned? Wh-question wh-word + be + subject + V-ed When was it built? The first auxiliary changes position: has it been fixed? / It hasn't been fixed. Form: by + agent Word Introduces Example by the doer The song was written by Adele. with a tool or material The door was opened with a key. by + agent goes at the end of the clause. The agent is added when it is new or important information. Form: two objects Subject Pattern Example The person person + be + V-ed + noun She was given a prize. The thing noun + be + V-ed + to + person A prize was given to her. These verbs allow both passives: give / send / offer / show / tell / teach / pay / lend. The person as the subject is the more usual choice. Passives with verb patterns Verb Form Example Phrasal verbs be looked after / be called off / be put off The children were looked after by their grandmother. / The match was called off. Prepositional verbs be dealt with / be waited for / be laughed at The problem was dealt with quickly. Verb, object and to-infinitive be + V-ed + to + base verb She was told to sit down. / The guests were asked to wait. make, see and hear be + made / seen / heard + to + base verb He was made to wait. / She was seen to leave. make, see and hear take the base verb in the active and to in the passive: They made him wait. → He was made to wait. Reporting passives Pattern Meaning Example It + be + V-ed + that + clause reports what people say or think It is said that he is rich. subject + be + V-ed + to + base verb the same time as the report He is believed to be the winner. subject + be + V-ed + to have + past participle an earlier time than the report He is said to have left the country. These verbs form reporting passives: say / think / believe / know / report / expect / consider / understand / claim / allege. Get passive Use Example an event that happens to someone, often unwanted He got hurt in the match. / Two men got arrested. a change of state or status She got promoted last year. / They got married in May. The get passive is informal. The be passive suits formal writing. He got arrested. = He was arrested. Negatives and questions use do: Did she get promoted? Use Use Example The doer is unknown My phone was stolen on the train. The doer is obvious or unimportant The room is cleaned every day. Processes and how things are made Wine is made from grapes. News, notices and formal writing Two people were arrested last night. The receiver is the topic Our teacher was given a prize. Passive in formal and academic writing Pattern Use Example It + be + V-ed + that + clause reports a finding or a decision It was found that the samples were damaged. It + be + V-ed + that + clause makes a request or a rule formal It is requested that visitors sign in. noun + be + V-ed method and process: the doer does not matter The samples were heated to 80 degrees. Choosing the passive Reason Example known information first, new information last We visited the museum. It was designed by a young architect. a long doer goes at the end The prize was won by a team of students from three universities. the same subject across sentences Anna joined the firm in May. She was promoted within a year. Need and want with -ing Pattern Meaning Example need + V-ing needs to be done The car needs washing. want / deserve / bear + V-ing wants, deserves or can take being done Your hair wants cutting. (US: needs cutting) / His words bear repeating. Compare: state and event State Event a result that exists now; the participle works as an adjective an action that someone does The door is closed now. The door was closed by the guard. The window is broken. The window was broken by a ball. very and quite can modify a participle used as an adjective. She is very worried. Middle voice Pattern Use Example noun + V-s + adverb a quality of the subject This book reads well. / Cotton washes easily. noun + won't + base verb the subject resists The door won't open. noun + be + V-ing a fixed phrase with an active form The film is showing at the Odeon. (US: is playing) A middle verb is active and names no doer; its meaning is passive. Stranded prepositions Pattern Use Example be + V-ed + preposition the preposition stays after the participle The proposal was agreed to. / This bed has been slept in. be + not to be + V-ed + preposition should not be done or cannot be done He is not to be relied on. Reporting passives: perfect and continuous Pattern Meaning Example subject + be + V-ed + to be + V-ing in progress at the time of the report She is believed to be working abroad. subject + be + V-ed + to have been + V-ing in progress before the report He is believed to have been living abroad. subject + be + V-ed + to have been + V-ed a passive action before the report The house is thought to have been built in 1800. There + be + V-ed + to be + noun reports that something exists There are said to be over a hundred. Typical errors English speaks here. English is spoken here. the subject receives the action → be + V-ed The bridge built in 1990. The bridge was built in 1990. the passive needs be The window was broke. The window was broken. use the past participle The accident was happened yesterday. The accident happened yesterday. happen, arrive and die have no passive The book was written from Orwell. The book was written by Orwell. agent → by Was the room cleaned? — Yes, it cleaned. Yes, it was. the short answer repeats be The road is repairing now. The road is being repaired now. am + is + are + being + V-ed is the present continuous passive He is said that he is rich. It is said that he is rich. / He is said to be rich. that follows It; a personal subject takes to The children were looked. The children were looked after. the particle stays after the participle He was made wait. He was made to wait. make takes to in the passive He was got arrested. He got arrested. get takes the place of be The car needs to wash. The car needs washing. / The car needs to be washed. need takes an -ing form or to be and a participle
