fixture.body: Inside a noun clause the subject comes before the verb, as in a statement: I know where she lives. / Tell me what you want. Point Rule Example That-clause that + subject + verb; that drops after common verbs I know (that) he left. Wh-clause wh-word + subject + verb; no do, does or did Tell me where he lives. If and whether if or whether after ask and wonder; whether after a preposition or to I wonder whether she knows. Wh-word and to wh-word + to + V I don't know what to do. Embedded question a polite question starts Could you tell me and keeps statement order Could you tell me where the station is? -ever words words in -ever mean any person, thing, time, place or way that Take whatever you like. Exclamation what or how opens it; the subject comes before the verb I can't believe how beautiful it is. Noun and clause the noun names what the clause says: the fact that, the question whether Despite the fact that it was late, we stayed. After be The problem is, This is why, That's what + clause The problem is where to park. After a preposition a wh-word or whether follows; before that the preposition drops It depends on whether we can park. Verbs of demand insist / demand / recommend + that + subject + base verb; British English often adds should She recommends that he rest. Trap a noun clause keeps statement order, with no do I don't know where the station is. Overview Function Example Subject What she said surprised me. Object I know that he left. Complement The problem is that we have no money. After a preposition I'm interested in what you think. A noun clause has its own subject and verb and does the work of a noun phrase. I know the answer. / I know what she said. Reported statements and questions are noun clauses. See Reported Speech. Form: that-clauses Follows Common words Example A verb believe / say / know / hope / decide / realise / discover I realised that I had lost my keys. An adjective afraid / certain / glad / sure / aware / surprised I'm glad that you came. A noun idea / fact / news / hope / belief / claim We heard the news that she had won. That is optional after common verbs and adjectives, and speech usually drops it. I hope (that) you feel better. Formal verbs and nouns keep that. The report states that prices fell. / He has the idea that it is easy. That-clauses as subject Pattern Example That + clause + verb That he left surprised me. It + verb + person + that + clause It surprised me that he left. It + is + adjective + that + clause It is clear that she is tired. A that-clause subject sounds formal; speech prefers it first. Form: wh-clauses Pattern Rule Example wh-word + subject + verb statement order, with no do, does or did Tell me where he lives. wh-word + verb the wh-word is the subject, so the verb follows it I wonder who called. wh-clause + singular verb a wh-clause as subject takes a singular verb What he does is his business. / What they need is more time. Embedded questions Change Direct question Embedded question The subject goes before the verb Where is the station? Could you tell me where the station is? do, does and did drop What time does it start? Do you know what time it starts? if or whether replaces the inversion Is she at home? I wonder whether she is at home. Use Example A polite request for information Could you tell me how much this costs? A question to someone who may know Do you know who is coming? A doubt, or a question to yourself I wonder why she left. Not knowing I have no idea when the shop opens. Wh-words with to Pattern Example wh-word + to + V I don't know what to do. = I don't know what I should do. whether + to + V We can't decide whether to go. = We can't decide whether we should go. The to-clause has no subject; the doer is the subject or the object of the main verb. She doesn't know where to park. / He told me where to park. The verbs that take these phrases are listed in Gerund vs Infinitive. Compare: if and whether Point if whether After ask, wonder, know, find out I wonder if she knows. I wonder whether she knows. After a preposition It depends on whether it rains. Before a to-infinitive I can't decide whether to go. At the start of a sentence Whether she agrees doesn't matter. Right before or not I'll ask whether or not she agrees. If is more usual in speech; whether is more usual in formal writing. A noun-clause if reports a question; a conditional if sets a condition. I wonder if it will rain. ≠ I stay in if it rains. Conditional clauses are in Conditionals. Words in -ever Word Meaning Example whoever any person who I'll talk to whoever is in charge. whatever anything that Take whatever you like. whichever any one that Choose whichever is cheaper. whenever at any time that Call me whenever you want. wherever in any place that Sit wherever you like. however in any way that Do it however you want. Exclamative clauses Pattern Example what + a + noun + subject + verb What a mess it was! / I can't believe what a mess it is. how + adjective + subject + verb How cold it is! / I can't believe how beautiful it is. how + adverb + subject + verb How fast he runs! / Did you see how fast he runs? Appositive clauses Phrase Use Example the + fact / idea / claim / belief + that + clause the noun names what the clause says The claim that prices will fall is false. the question + whether + clause question takes whether The question whether we can afford it remains. despite the fact that although Despite the fact that it was late, we stayed. in view of the fact that because of; formal In view of the fact that prices rose, we waited. An appositive clause names the noun's content; a relative that clause has a gap and can become which. the news that she won ≠ the news that she told us Wh-clauses after be Use Example A problem or question: The problem is, The question is The problem is where to park. / The question is whether we can afford it. A reason: This is why This is why I called. A way: That's how That's how it works. A place: This is where This is where we met. A thing meant: That's what That's what I mean. Clauses after prepositions and adjectives Phrase Example aware / sure + of + wh-word She is aware of how much it costs. / I'm not sure of what he meant. depends on + whether + clause It depends on whether we can park. the extent + to which + clause The report shows the extent to which prices have risen. in what way + clause She asked in what way the plan had failed. Before a that-clause the preposition drops, or the fact carries it. She is aware that it closed. = She is aware of the fact that it closed. Compare: free relative and interrogative clauses Point Free relative Interrogative Meaning what = the thing that what = which thing Example I eat what she cooks. I wonder what she cooks. Test replace what with the thing that turn the clause into a direct question Result I eat the food that she cooks. What does she cook? Verbs such as know, remember and see take both kinds; the test shows which a sentence means. I remember what she said. That-clauses after verbs of demand Pattern Rule Example verb + that + subject + base verb the subjunctive: the base verb for every subject The manager demanded that he apologise. verb + that + subject + should + base verb the usual British form The manager demanded that he should apologise. verb + that + subject + should not / not + base verb negative: not before the verb, with no do We suggest that he should not wait. / We suggest that he not wait. Verbs of demand and advice take it: insist, demand, require, request, suggest, recommend, propose. Adjectives such as essential take the same clause. See The Subjunctive. Typical errors I don't know where is the station. I don't know where the station is. the subject goes before the verb in a noun clause Tell me what do you want. Tell me what you want. a noun clause takes no do She asked me if or not I was ready. She asked me whether or not I was ready. or not right after the word takes whether I can't decide if to go. I can't decide whether to go. whether goes before a to-infinitive What he does are his business. What he does is his business. a wh-clause as subject takes a singular verb Despite he was tired, he came. Despite the fact that he was tired, he came. despite takes a noun phrase or the fact that The problem is where do we park. The problem is where we park. a wh-clause after be keeps statement order He is afraid of that he will fail. He is afraid that he will fail. the preposition drops before that The question that we can afford it remains. The question whether we can afford it remains. question takes whether I am aware about how much it costs. I am aware of how much it costs. aware takes of before a wh-clause

Trap じゃありません already ends the sentence; add no です. たなかさんは先生じゃありません。 Tanaka-san is not a teacher. Overview noun + は + noun + です means “A is B”. わたしはアンナです。 I'm Anna. です stays the same for every person and number. わたしはがくせいです。 / わたしたちはがくせいです。 I am a student. / We are students. です belongs to the polite form: use it with strangers, at school and at work. は is a particle that marks the topic; it is read わ. See は and が. あります and います say that something exists or where it is. See あります and います. です also ends a sentence with an adjective. See い-Adjectives and な-Adjectives. Casual speech uses the plain form だ in place of です. See The Plain Form. Introducing yourself Use Example Meeting someone for the first time はじめまして。 Nice to meet you. Giving your name わたしはジョンです。 I'm John. Giving only your name ジョンです。 I'm John. Closing an introduction よろしくおねがいします。 I look forward to getting along with you. A whole introduction はじめまして。わたしはアンナです。よろしくおねがいします。 — はじめまして。たなかです。よろしくおねがいします。 Nice to meet you. I'm Anna. I look forward to getting along with you. — Nice to meet you. I'm Tanaka. I look forward to getting along with you. さん follows another person's name; your own name takes none. わたしはアンナです。 / たなかさんはせんせいです。 I'm Anna. / Tanaka-san is a teacher. Form: polite present and past Tense Affirmative Negative Present noun + です noun + じゃありません Past noun + でした noun + じゃありませんでした The negative takes じゃありません in place of です. 私は学生じゃありません。 I am not a student. The past is でした; the negative past is じゃありませんでした. きのうはやすみでした。 / きのうはやすみじゃありませんでした。 Yesterday was a day off. / Yesterday was not a day off. A past form goes with a time word such as きのう (“yesterday”) or むかし (“long ago”). むかし、私は学生でした。 I was a student once. Form: questions and answers Form Example noun + は + noun + ですか アンナさんは学生ですか。 Is Anna a student? Answer: yes アンナさんは学生ですか。 — はい、学生です。 Is Anna a student? — Yes, she is a student. Answer: no たなかさんは先生ですか。 — いいえ、先生じゃありません。 Is Tanaka-san a teacher? — No, he is not a teacher. Past きのうはやすみでしたか。 — はい、やすみでした。 Was yesterday a day off? — Yes, it was. か at the end of the sentence makes a question; the word order does not change. Question words and question intonation: see Questions. Use Use Example What a thing is これはほんです。 This is a book. Someone's name わたしのなまえはアンナです。 My name is Anna. Who someone is to you アンナさんは私のともだちです。 Anna is my friend. Job or status たなかさんは先生です。 / アンナさんは学生です。 Tanaka-san is a teacher. / Anna is a student. Nationality アンナさんはアメリカ人です。 / たなかさんは日本人です。 Anna is American. / Tanaka-san is Japanese. も replaces は for “too”: noun + も + noun + です. See Particles と, も, の. 私も学生です。 I'm a student too. Finer points Point Example じゃありません: conversation and everyday writing これは私の本じゃありません。 This is not my book. ではありません: writing, speeches and announcements これは私の本ではありません。 / きのうはやすみではありませんでした。 This is not my book. / Yesterday was not a day off. A topic that is clear from the situation is left out; です stays アンナです。学生です。 I'm Anna. I'm a student. そうです confirms the question たなかさんは先生ですか。 — はい、そうです。 Is Tanaka-san a teacher? — Yes, that's right. ちがいます or そうじゃありません denies it たなかさんは先生ですか。 — いいえ、ちがいます。 Is Tanaka-san a teacher? — No, that's not right. After いいえ, the correct noun with です gives the answer アンナさんは先生ですか。 — いいえ、学生です。 Is Anna a teacher? — No, she is a student. Typical errors わたしはアンナさんです。 わたしはアンナです。 さん follows the name of another person, never your own 私は学生じゃありませんです。 私は学生じゃありません。 じゃありません already closes the sentence; です does not follow きのうはやすみじゃありません。 きのうはやすみじゃありませんでした。 a past time word needs a past form: じゃありませんでした 私は学生です。私はアメリカ人です。 私は学生です。アメリカ人です。 once the topic is clear, 私は is left out; English needs “I” in every sentence, Japanese does not

fixture.lead: は marks what the sentence is about; が marks a new subject or the one a question word asks for.

fixture.body: What is known takes は; what is new takes が: ここに本があります。その本は大きいです。 Point Rule Example Topic noun + は + clause アンナさんは学生です。 Anna is a student. Subject noun + が + verb たなかさんが来ました。 Tanaka-san has come. Known or new The new thing takes が; next time it is known and takes は. ここに本があります。その本は大きいです。 There is a book here. That book is big. Question word As the subject it takes が, and so does its answer. だれが来ましたか。 — たなかさんが来ました。 Who has come? — Tanaka-san has come. Contrast は sets one thing against another. ごはんは食べますが、パンは食べません。 I eat rice, but I don't eat bread. After a particle は follows another particle: では, には. ここでは食べません。 I don't eat here. Trap Introduce yourself with は, not が. 私はアンナです。 I'm Anna. Trap すき takes が for the thing liked, not を. 私はねこがすきです。 I like cats. Overview は marks the topic, what the sentence is about: noun + は + clause. アンナさんは学生です。 Anna is a student. が marks the subject, who or what does or is something: noun + が + verb. バスが来ました。 The bus has come. The particle は is read わ. See Hiragana. A sentence with です takes its topic with は. See です: Am, Is, Are. も replaces は and が for “also”. See Particles と, も, の. は: the topic Use Example Who or what the sentence is about, with です たなかさんは先生です。 Tanaka-san is a teacher. The topic of a verb アンナさんはテレビを見ます。 Anna watches TV. The topic of an adjective この本は大きいです。 This book is big. A time as the topic あしたはやすみです。 Tomorrow is a day off. The topic of a question あなたは学生ですか。 Are you a student? One topic for several sentences アンナさんは学生です。日本語をべんきょうします。 Anna is a student. She studies Japanese. The topic stands first in the sentence. See Word Order. が: the subject Use Example Something new happens あ、たなかさんが来ました。 Oh, Tanaka-san has come. Something new exists; see あります and います ここに本があります。 There is a book here. A new person enters a story むかし、おじいさんがいました。 Long ago there was an old man. Question words with が A question word that is the subject takes が; the answer that replaces it takes が too. Use Example Who does it? だれが来ましたか。 — たなかさんが来ました。 Who has come? — Tanaka-san has come. What exists? 何がありますか。 — 本があります。 What is there? — There is a book. Which one is it? だれが学生ですか。 — アンナさんが学生です。 Who is the student? — Anna is the student. A known topic and a question word: は on the topic あの人はだれですか。 — たなかさんです。 Who is that person? — It is Tanaka-san. The question words and the answers to yes-no questions: see Questions. Compare: は and が Known to both speakers: は. New, or picked from several: が. Use Example The same words answer two questions アンナさんは学生です。 / アンナさんが学生です。 Anna is a student. / It is Anna who is a student. First mention, then the known thing ここに本があります。その本は大きいです。 There is a book here. That book is big. は for contrast は replaces が and を, and follows other particles: では, には. Use Example Two things set side by side ごはんは食べますが、パンは食べません。 I eat rice, but I don't eat bread. A negative that leaves other things open さかなは食べません。 Fish I don't eat. A place set against other places ここでは食べません。 I don't eat here. Two topics, two comments 私は学生です。アンナさんは先生です。 I am a student. Anna is a teacher. は and が in one sentence は names the person; が names the thing liked, wanted or mastered. See Likes and Wants: 好き, ほしい. Use Example Liking 私はねこがすきです。 I like cats. Wanting アンナさんはくるまがほしいです。 Anna wants a car. Being good at something アンナさんは日本語がじょうずです。 Anna is good at Japanese. Typical errors 私がアンナです。 私はアンナです。 a self-introduction names the topic with は; が would say “I am the one who is Anna” だれは来ましたか。 だれが来ましたか。 a question word that is the subject takes が 私はねこをすきです。 私はねこがすきです。 すき takes が for the thing liked; the thing is not an object ごはんが食べますが、パンが食べません。 ごはんは食べますが、パンは食べません。 two things set against each other take は

fixture.title: Questions
fixture.lead: か turns a sentence into a question; question words such as なん, だれ and どこ stand where the answer will stand.

fixture.body: Add か at the end; the word order stays the same: これはほんですか。 Point Rule Example Pattern noun + は + noun + ですか これはほんですか。 Is this a book? Question word It takes the place of the answer; か still ends the sentence. これはなんですか。 — ペンです。 What is this? — It is a pen. Words なん “what”, だれ “who”, どこ “where”. トイレはどこですか。 — あそこです。 Where is the toilet? — Over there. Answers はい “yes”, いいえ “no”, then the answer. はい、ほんです。 / いいえ、ノートです。 Yes, it is a book. / No, it is a notebook. Intonation The voice rises on か. これはほんですか。↗ Is this a book? More words いつ “when”, いくら “how much”, どれ “which”, どう “how”. この本はいくらですか。 — 800円です。 How much is this book? — It is 800 yen. Verbs The answer repeats the verb. あした日本へ行きますか。 — はい、行きます。 Are you going to Japan tomorrow? — Yes, I am. Subject A question word as the subject takes が. だれが来ますか。 — たなかさんが来ます。 Who is coming? — Tanaka-san is coming. Why どうして asks for a reason; the answer ends in から. どうしてきのう休みましたか。 — びょうきでしたから。 Why were you absent from school yesterday? — Because I was ill. Negative question はい agrees with the question as asked; いいえ corrects it. たなかさんは学生じゃありませんか。 — いいえ、学生です。 Isn’t Tanaka-san a student? — No, he is a student. Trap A polite question ends in か; rising voice alone is casual. あした日本へ行きますか。 Are you going to Japan tomorrow? Overview か at the end makes a question; the word order stays the same. これはほんですか。 Is this a book? A question word stands where the answer will stand; the rest of the sentence stays. これはほんです。 / これはなんですか。 This is a book. / What is this? A question word as the subject takes が. See は and が. Form: questions with か Form Example noun + は + noun + ですか これはほんですか。 Is this a book? noun + は + adjective + ですか そのラーメンはおいしいですか。 Is that ramen good? noun + でしたか きのうはあめでしたか。 Was it rainy yesterday? verb + ますか あした日本へ行きますか。 Are you going to Japan tomorrow? verb + ましたか 日本へ行きましたか。 Did you go to Japan? か follows the polite ending without a pause: ですか, ますか. The forms of ます are in The ます-Form; the past of です is in です: Am, Is, Are. Question words Word Meaning Example なん “what” これはなんですか。 — ペンです。 What is this? — It is a pen. だれ “who” あのひとはだれですか。 — たなかさんです。 Who is that person? — That is Tanaka-san. どこ “where” トイレはどこですか。 — あそこです。 Where is the toilet? — Over there. いつ “when” パーティーはいつですか。 — 土曜日です。 When is the party? — On Saturday. いくら “how much” (price) この本はいくらですか。 — 800円です。 How much is this book? — It is 800 yen. どれ “which” of three or more things あなたのかさはどれですか。 — あれです。 Which one is your umbrella? — That one over there. どう “how”, “what is it like” 日本のりょうりはどうですか。 — とてもおいしいです。 How is Japanese food? — Very tasty. 何時 “what time” 今、何時ですか。 — 三時です。 What time is it now? — It is three o’clock. どうして “why” どうしてきのう休みましたか。 — びょうきでしたから。 Why were you absent from school yesterday? — Because I was ill. なに becomes なん before です, の and counters, and stays なに before を, が and も; one kanji writes both. 何ですか。 / 何を食べますか。 What is this? / What do you eat? A question word as the subject takes が; the answer takes が too. だれが日本へ行きますか。 Who is going to Japan? どれ and its family どの, どこ, どちら are in こそあど: This, That, Which; the time in Telling the Time; the prices in Counters. Answers Answer Example Yes これはほんですか。 — はい、ほんです。 Is this a book? — Yes, it is a book. No これはほんですか。 — いいえ、ノートです。 Is this a book? — No, it is a notebook. Yes to a verb あした日本へ行きますか。 — はい、行きます。 Are you going to Japan tomorrow? — Yes, I am. No to a verb あした日本へ行きますか。 — いいえ、行きません。 Are you going to Japan tomorrow? — No, I am not. Agreeing with a negative question たなかさんは学生じゃありませんか。 — はい、学生じゃありません。 Isn’t Tanaka-san a student? — Right, he is not a student. Correcting a negative question たなかさんは学生じゃありませんか。 — いいえ、学生です。 Isn’t Tanaka-san a student? — No, he is a student. はい or いいえ comes first; the answer after it has no か. はい confirms what the question says, positive or negative; いいえ denies it. The short answers そうです and ちがいます are in です: Am, Is, Are. Pronunciation: intonation Form Example With か: the voice rises on か これはほんですか。↗ Is this a book? Casual speech without か: the voice rises on the last syllable コーヒー、飲む↗ — うん、飲む↘ Want some coffee? — Yeah, I do. In writing, a polite question ends in か and 。; ？ belongs to casual messages. See The Plain Form. Typical errors これはほんです？ これはほんですか。 a polite question ends in か; rising voice alone is casual だれは来ますか。 だれが来ますか。 a question word as the subject takes が, not は たなかさんは学生じゃありませんか。 — はい、学生です。 たなかさんは学生じゃありませんか。 — いいえ、学生です。 はい agrees with the negative question, so “he is a student” needs いいえ

fixture.body: Only the ending changes: 食べます / 食べません / 食べました / 食べませんでした Point Rule Example Present verb + ます 毎日、朝ごはんを食べます。 I eat breakfast every day. Negative verb + ません 朝ごはんを食べません。 I don't eat breakfast. Past verb + ました 今朝、朝ごはんを食べました。 I ate breakfast this morning. Past negative verb + ませんでした 今朝、朝ごはんを食べませんでした。 I didn't eat breakfast this morning. Question verb + ますか コーヒーを飲みますか。 — はい、飲みます。 Do you drink coffee? — Yes, I do. Tense ます covers habits, today and the future. 明日、学校に行きます。 Tomorrow I will go to school. Time words A past word goes with ました; 今日, 明日 and 昨日 take no particle. 昨日、えいがを見ました。 Yesterday I watched a film. Style Polite speech ends every sentence in です or ます. 私は学生です。毎日、日本語を勉強します。 I am a student. I study Japanese every day. Time words Weeks: 毎週 habit, 来週 next, 先週 last. 先週、日本に行きました。 I went to Japan last week. Trap ません closes the sentence; add no です. 朝ごはんを食べません。 I don't eat breakfast. Trap ます follows the stem, not the dictionary form. 毎朝、コーヒーを飲みます。 I drink coffee every morning. Overview The ます-form is the polite form of a verb: it ends the sentence and stays the same for every person. 私は毎朝、コーヒーを飲みます。 I drink coffee every morning. One form serves habits, the present and the future. 毎日、日本語を勉強します。 / 明日、学校に行きます。 I study Japanese every day. / Tomorrow I will go to school. How the ます-form is made from the dictionary form: see Verb Groups. Form: four endings Tense Affirmative Negative Present verb + ます verb + ません Past verb + ました verb + ませんでした Form Example ます 毎日、朝ごはんを食べます。 I eat breakfast every day. ません 朝ごはんを食べません。 I don't eat breakfast. ました 今朝、朝ごはんを食べました。 I ate breakfast this morning. ませんでした 今朝、朝ごはんを食べませんでした。 I didn't eat breakfast this morning. The negative ません and the past ました replace ます; the past negative is ませんでした. ませんか makes an invitation; see Invitations: ましょう and ませんか. Form: questions and answers Form Example Question and answer: yes コーヒーを飲みますか。 — はい、飲みます。 Do you drink coffee? — Yes, I do. Answer: no コーヒーを飲みますか。 — いいえ、飲みません。 Do you drink coffee? — No, I don't. Question in the past 昨日、勉強しましたか。 — はい、しました。 Did you study yesterday? — Yes, I did. With a question word 今日は何を食べますか。 — すしを食べます。 What are you going to eat today? — I will eat sushi. か at the end makes the question; the word order stays. See Questions. A short answer repeats the verb alone: はい with the question's form, いいえ with the negative. Time words Word Example 毎日 毎日、日本語を勉強します。 I study Japanese every day. 毎朝 毎朝、コーヒーを飲みます。 I drink coffee every morning. 今日 今日、しんぶんを読みます。 I will read the newspaper today. 明日 明日、学校に行きます。 Tomorrow I will go to school. 昨日 昨日、えいがを見ました。 Yesterday I watched a film. 今朝 今朝、パンを食べました。 I ate bread this morning. 毎週 毎週、土曜日にテニスをします。 I play tennis every Saturday. 来週 来週、日本に行きます。 I will go to Japan next week. 先週 先週、日本に行きました。 I went to Japan last week. A time word of the past goes with ました; habits, today and the future go with ます. A clock time takes に; 今日, 明日, 昨日 and words with 毎 take no particle. See Particles を, に, で, へ. 7時に起きます。 I get up at seven. Verbs of daily life Verb Example 食べます すしを食べます。 I will eat sushi. 飲みます 毎朝、コーヒーを飲みます。 I drink coffee every morning. 見ます テレビを見ます。 I watch TV. 読みます 今日、しんぶんを読みます。 I will read the newspaper today. 書きます てがみを書きます。 I write a letter. 買います スーパーでパンを買います。 I buy bread at the supermarket. 話します 先生と日本語を話します。 I speak Japanese with the teacher. 行きます 明日、学校に行きます。 Tomorrow I will go to school. 来ます ともだちが来ます。 A friend is coming. 帰ります 6時にうちへ帰ります。 I go home at six. 起きます 7時に起きます。 I get up at seven. ねます 11時にねます。 I go to bed at eleven. 勉強します 毎日、日本語を勉強します。 I study Japanese every day. します 毎週、土曜日にテニスをします。 I play tennis every Saturday. Use Use Example Strangers, shops, offices このバスはえきに行きますか。 — はい、行きます。 Does this bus go to the station? — Yes, it does. Teachers and people you respect 先生、明日、学校に来ますか。 Teacher, will you come to school tomorrow? A polite text keeps です and ます through every sentence. 私は学生です。毎日、日本語を勉強します。 I am a student. I study Japanese every day. Friends and family use the plain form instead; see The Plain Form. Typical errors 朝ごはんを食べませんです。 朝ごはんを食べません。 ません already closes the sentence; です does not follow 朝ごはんを食べないます。 朝ごはんを食べません。 the negative is ません; ない belongs to the plain form コーヒーを飲むます。 コーヒーを飲みます。 ます follows the stem 飲み, not the dictionary form 飲む; see Verb Groups 今朝、朝ごはんを食べますでした。 今朝、朝ごはんを食べました。 the past is ました; でした belongs to nouns with です 明日に学校へ行きます。 明日、学校へ行きます。 今日, 明日 and 昨日 take no particle 私は学生です。毎日、日本語を勉強する。 私は学生です。毎日、日本語を勉強します。 a text keeps one style: です goes with ます, not with the plain form

fixture.body: Only the last verb carries the tense; the others take the て-form: 食べて、行きます。 Point Rule Example Group 2 る → て 朝ごはんを食べて、学校へ行きます。 I eat breakfast and go to school. Group 1: う, つ, る う・つ・る → って 本を買って、うちへ帰ります。 I buy a book and go home. Group 1: む, ぶ, ぬ む・ぶ・ぬ → んで コーヒーを飲んで、本を読みます。 I drink coffee and read a book. Group 1: く, ぐ く → いて / ぐ → いで ノートに書いて、おぼえます。 / プールでおよいで、シャワーをあびます。 I write it in my notebook and memorise it. / I swim in the pool and take a shower. Group 1: す す → して たなかさんと話して、帰ります。 I talk with Tanaka-san and go home. Irregular する → して / 来る → 来て アンナさんが来て、いっしょにごはんを食べます。 Anna comes and we eat together. Sequence Only the last verb shows the tense. きのう、朝ごはんを食べて、学校へ行きました。 Yesterday I ate breakfast and went to school. After verb + て + から しゅくだいをしてから、テレビを見ます。 After I do my homework, I watch TV. Trap 行く is an exception: it takes って. 駅へ行って、アンナさんに会います。 I go to the station and meet Anna. Trap The て-form starts from the dictionary form. ジュースを飲んで、ねます。 I drink juice and go to bed. Overview Only the last verb of a sequence shows tense and politeness; the others take the て-form. きのう、朝ごはんを食べて、学校へ行きました。 Yesterday I ate breakfast and went to school. The て-form has one shape for every person, number and style of speech. The て-form is built from the dictionary form; the group of the verb decides the change. See Verb Groups. The て-form is the base of requests, see Requests: てください, and of actions in progress and states, see ています: Actions and States. More patterns with the て-form: permission and prohibition, see Permission and Obligation: May, Must. Form: making the て-form Dictionary ending Change Example Group 2 る → て 食べる → 食べて / 見る → 見て Group 1: う, つ, る う・つ・る → って 買う → 買って / 待つ → 待って / 帰る → 帰って Group 1: む, ぶ, ぬ む・ぶ・ぬ → んで 飲む → 飲んで / 読む → 読んで / あそぶ → あそんで Group 1: く く → いて 書く → 書いて / 聞く → 聞いて Group 1: ぐ ぐ → いで およぐ → およいで / いそぐ → いそいで Group 1: す す → して 話す → 話して / かす → かして Irregular する・来る → して・来て する → して / 来る → 来て Irregular 行く → 行って 行く → 行って The plain past た-form changes the same way: 食べて gives 食べた. See The Plain Form. Use Use Example Two actions in a row スーパーへ行って、パンを買います。 I go to the supermarket and buy bread. Three actions or more 朝起きて、ごはんを食べて、学校へ行きます。 In the morning I get up, eat and go to school. After an action: verb + て + から しゅくだいをしてから、テレビを見ます。 After I do my homework, I watch TV. The way an action is done 駅まで歩いて行きます。 I walk to the station. Going to do something and coming back パンを買って来ます。 I'll go and buy some bread and come back. Adjectives link in their own way: くて after an い-adjective, で after a な-adjective. See い-Adjectives and な-Adjectives. Typical errors 朝ごはんを食べるて、行きます。 朝ごはんを食べて、行きます。 the る of the dictionary form is replaced by て, not followed by it コーヒーを飲みて、本を読みます。 コーヒーを飲んで、本を読みます。 む, ぶ and ぬ become んで; the ます-stem takes no て 駅へ行いて、アンナさんに会います。 駅へ行って、アンナさんに会います。 行く is an exception: って, not いて プールでおよいて、シャワーをあびます。 プールでおよいで、シャワーをあびます。 after ぐ the ending is voiced: いで きのう、朝ごはんを食べて、学校へ行きます。 きのう、朝ごはんを食べて、学校へ行きました。 the last verb carries the tense for the whole sequence
